title: Ang 1245–1251: Sarang ki Var ends
tomorrow: a form asks: a roommate of your own faith? what does she tick?

lines: A GURU, ASKING FOR A DONATION.
ANG 1245: DON'T BOW AT HIS FEET.
IF NOT THE TITLE, THEN WHAT?
cards: Somewhere online right now, a man with very good lighting calls himself a guru and asks for a donation to unlock lesson two. Here's the odd part.

Open a book whose authors are all called Guru, turn to ang 1245, and Guru Nanak warns about exactly that. In paraphrase: someone who calls himself a guru or a pir and goes around begging, don't bow at his feet.
A Guru, telling you to be careful of gurus. So if the title proves nothing, what does?

teach.h: THE NEXT LINE GIVES THE TEST.
teach.b: The very next line answers, and it isn't about titles at all.

teach.h: EARN, EAT, GIVE FROM YOUR HAND.
teach.b: In paraphrase: one who works for what he eats, and gives some of it from his own hand, Nanak says, that one recognizes the path. Ghaal khaae, kichh hathahu dee. Earn, eat, give.
That's the puzzle solved. The test is in the hands, not the robe. A title costs nothing to claim.
Sweat and sharing are hard to fake.

teach.h: GURU OR PIR: THE SAME TEST.
teach.b: Notice, too, that the line names two titles, guru and pir, a Sufi teacher, and holds them both to the same test.
Sikhs hear in it the shape of an ordinary honest life: kirat karni, earning by honest work, and vand chhakna, sharing what you have. Here's something to tell a friend tonight.
The line doesn't say never give to someone who asks.
It warns against bowing to a teacher who makes himself one and lives off others, and then praises the person whose hand points outward.
That's how the ballad's second half opens, and from here Guru Ram Das's pauris carry it to the end, on ang 1251.
Simran picked up her last paycheck from her dad's dispatch office yesterday, and it's sitting on her desk. Earned, yes. Eaten, mostly, in gas and snacks.
And the third word is still waiting.

how: Sikhs speak of earning by honest work (kirat karni) and sharing (vand chhakna) as part of daily life; some set aside a portion of their earnings to give, and readers turn to this line on ang 1245 for it.

o: where the ballad's second half tests a teacher
where Guru Nanak opens the morning raga
where Kabir's hymns in raga Sarang begin

games.q: the line on ang 1245 — tap the pairs.
p: give some from your own hand
a title for a Sufi teacher

s: the line on ang 1245 says never give to anyone who asks
it warns against bowing to a self-made guru who begs, and praises the one who gives.
in this line, the test of the path is in the hands, not the title
work for what you eat, give some from your hand: that one recognizes the path.
in Sikh teaching, earning money gets in the way of the path
the line puts honest work inside the path: earn, eat, give.

games.q: an account you follow says real seekers 'invest' in his course to unlock his blessings. with ang 1245 in mind, what do you weigh first?
o: how he lives: by his own work, and with an open hand.
his title: if he's called a guru, he must be one.
his price: the more it costs, the more real it is.
games.why: Guru Nanak's test is the hands: one who works for what he eats and gives from his own hand recognizes the path. the title alone proves nothing.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up, and let the breath slow down. These are the hands that work, that feed you, that can give.
With each out-breath, quietly bring to mind one thing they did this week for someone else, however small. If you'd like, read ang 1245 first.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1245. Where Sarang ki Var's second half begins: not the title but the hands. Work, eat, and give some from your own hand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: 'works and eats', the opening of the line on ang 1245.

carryVoice: For the road: the ballad ends on hands, not titles: earn, eat, give a little. Back tomorrow.
